lead: This page is a how-to. Lead with the shortest path from nothing to `{keyword}` working.
extract: **Commands verbatim.** Flag names, argument order and quoting exactly as written. A paraphrased flag is a wrong flag. Where the page gives no runnable command for this, say so -- a command assembled in the style of the ones it does give reads exactly like one the vendor published.

**Prerequisites, swept from the whole page.** This is where a how-to costs someone an afternoon: it describes the happy path and states its setup somewhere other than in the steps -- an earlier page in the series, a note, a parenthesis, a callout. Name each exactly: package and version, an API to enable, an IAM role string, a permission, a machine or accelerator type, an environment variable. A prerequisite discovered at step 4 costs the whole run.
**Result.** What comes back, in what form, and where it appears. If it lands somewhere the command does not make obvious, that location *is* the finding.
**Constraints.** Whatever would make these steps not work: a version floor, where a component has to run, what it cannot reach, a platform excluded.
trap: A how-to is written for the case where everything is already in place, so the thing that will stop the reader is rarely in the steps. Prefer the parenthetical over the numbered list when deciding what matters.
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by being *plausible* -- the steps read fine and the run dies at the one the page never actually gave.

lead: This is a reference page. If `{keyword}` names one flag, option or symbol here, **that is the entry**: give it the top section in full and cover the rest only where it bears on that one. Report the whole surface only if `{keyword}` is the page itself.
extract: **Exact spelling.** These pages document a CLI and a Python surface at once -- `--max-num-seqs` and `max_num_seqs` -- and the two are not interchangeable at the point of use. Give the form for each surface shown.
**Type**, and the **default as this page states it**.
**What it controls**, in the page's own terms.

**What it interacts with.** The part a reader cannot reconstruct and the part that costs them: a value silently capped by another, one that takes effect only when a third is set, one whose useful range depends on something in a different section.
Anything marked **required, deprecated or experimental**.
trap_title: The trap: a default is a default for a version
trap:
These pages document the tip of a moving branch; defaults change between releases and several differ by hardware backend. Give the default as written, note the version the page documents, and say nothing about what it used to be or is elsewhere.

Two refusals. **Do not infer an option from a sibling** -- these pages are generated, so options come in families that look regular right up to the one that is not. **Do not complete a name you can only see truncated.**
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by being *confidently specific*: the name is nearly right, the default is last year's, and nothing about it looks uncertain.

lead: This page explains a mechanism. These pages cover a whole subsystem; lead with `{keyword}`'s role in it and bring in the surrounding machinery only as far as is needed to make that role make sense.
extract: **Mechanism.** What actually happens, in order, in the page's own vocabulary. Prefer its names over your own: `{keyword}` has a precise meaning in this document and a fuzzier one in general use, and the precise one is the whole reason to have an entry.

**What it constrains.** The reason anybody reads a concept page is to find out what it stops them doing: sizes that must divide, memory not addressable from where they are, an operation that forces a barrier, a shape that must be static, a resource that is per-core rather than per-chip. State each as a constraint on the reader's code, not as a property of the hardware in the abstract.
**Units and scope, every time.** A quantity here is per-core, per-chip, per-host or per-slice, and the page often says which only once, far from the number. Carry the unit with the figure.

**What the page does not settle.** Required, not optional: the quantities it illustrates but does not specify, the behaviour it describes for one case and does not generalise, the thing it says depends on something it never gives.
trap_title: The trap: a concept page is not a spec
trap: Its numbers are illustrative -- chosen to make an example legible, correct for the configuration the author had in mind, and not a commitment. Read as a spec, that is how a plausible number reaches a roofline and makes the whole model wrong while the arithmetic still checks out. Naming what the page leaves open is what stops the entry being quoted as more than it is.
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by being *coherent* -- a smooth causal account, assembled from a page that was describing two separate cases.

lead: This page carries the hardware numbers for `{keyword}`. They are the denominators every roofline divides by: wrong by 2x here and every ceiling built on this entry is wrong by 2x, silently, because the arithmetic still checks out.
extract: **Peak compute** -- bf16 and FP8 where both are given; say if a figure is sparse rather than dense.
**HBM** -- capacity and bandwidth, separately.
**TensorCores / SparseCores per chip** -- counts, and note if the chip is multi-chiplet with separate memory spaces, because that changes what a device is to the framework.
**ICI / DCN** -- bandwidth, and what it connects.
**Pod** -- maximum chips, and any constraint on valid slice shapes.
**Host VM** -- machine type, chips per host, vCPU and RAM.
**Frameworks** -- only those the page explicitly marks unsupported. An absence is not an exclusion.
Every row of the table stays. `not stated` is the correct value wherever the page is silent: it tells the next reader the page was checked.
trap:
Vendor pages quote peak compute per *chip*; a roofline usually wants it per *TensorCore*, and a chip has more than one. The same ambiguity runs through the table -- HBM figures are per chip, core counts per chip, ICI bandwidth may be per link or per chip -- and the page often states which exactly once, in a heading or footnote far from the figure.

Every value therefore carries its unit *and its denominator*, in the page's own words: `2307 TFLOPs bf16 per chip`, not `2307 TFLOPs`. Where the page gives a figure and never says per what, write the figure and `denominator not stated`. That is a useful entry; a figure with a denominator you supplied is not.

**Never carry a figure from another generation.** These pages are near-identical in layout and differ in exactly the numbers, so a borrowed value is invisible in a filled table and wrong in every calculation downstream.
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by being *complete* -- a full table, every cell plausible, one of them belonging to a different chip.

lead: This page documents profiling on Cloud TPU. Behind these keywords there is almost always one concrete question -- *how do I get a hosted xprof link for a run on this cluster* -- so lead with whatever moves someone toward that and treat the product tour as background.
extract: **The name mapping, once.** The product is Google Cloud ML Diagnostics in the documentation, but on a GKE cluster it presents as `managedMachineLearningDiagnostics` and a `gke-managed-mldiagnostics` namespace. Write in the page's public vocabulary and say once which cluster-side names it corresponds to -- that mapping is what connects the docs to what `kubectl` shows.
**Commands verbatim**, including the release track (`alpha`, `beta`) and every flag name.

**Enablement, in order.** These features need several things true at once and the page usually lists them apart from the steps: an API enabled, an IAM role granted, a cluster-level setting, a label on the workload or namespace, a bucket. Name role strings and label keys character for character, and say which are one-time cluster setup versus per-run.
**What you get back, and where you look at it.** If the result is only reachable from a particular Console page, that is the finding, because it is what someone cannot guess.
trap_title: The trap: the stack contradicts these docs
trap:
Two cautions, both of which cost hours:

- If the page shows a PyTorch collector as `torch_xla.debug.profiler.start_server(...)`, **report it as written** -- it is what the page says. Then note, as a caveat *outside* the quoted snippet, that the TPU images in use here ship `torch_tpu` and no `torch_xla`, so that import raises `ModuleNotFoundError` and the equivalent is `torch_tpu._internal.profiler.start_server(...)`. Never substitute inside a quotation: a doctored quote is worse than either version alone.
- If traces are written to Cloud Storage from the workload, note that this needs the node pool's OAuth scope to permit storage writes. That is fixed at node-pool creation and no amount of IAM will produce it -- which is why this failure looks like a permissions problem and is not one.
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by being *faithful to the page and wrong in the pod* -- every command correct as documented, against an image that does not have the module.

lead: This is a `gcloud` command reference. Report its surface, not its prose: the command groups and subcommands it lists, and for each the required positional arguments and flags, spelled exactly as the page spells them.
extract: **Subcommands**, and for each its required positionals and its flags.
**Flag names character for character**, with any default the page states.
Anything marked **required**, and anything the page marks deprecated.
**The release track.** This is under `alpha`.
trap:
A command that exists in one track can be absent or renamed in another, and that surfaces as `unrecognized arguments` rather than as a permissions error -- so it gets debugged as the wrong problem. Record the track with the command, every time.

Do not infer a flag from a sibling command, and do not complete a flag name you can only see truncated.
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by being *nearly runnable* -- the right command in the wrong track, which fails in a way that looks like anything but that.

lead: This is a repository landing page: a README rendered as the front door to a codebase. It is an orientation document, not a manual. Lead with what the project *is* and what problem it exists for, then how a reader gets in -- install, the first command, the entry point. Say plainly where the README stops, because on a landing page that boundary is most of what a reader needs from you.
extract: **What it is, in the project's own words.** A README's first paragraph is the only place the authors say what they think they built. Quote or closely follow it rather than characterising the project yourself; a summary written from the file tree describes a directory, not a project.

**How to get in.** Install line, first runnable command, and the entry point a reader starts from, each exactly as written. If the page gives no runnable command, say so -- one assembled from the style of the others reads exactly like one the project published.
**The map.** Which directory holds what, where the examples are, where the tests are. This is the part a landing page is uniquely good for and the part a reader cannot get from a search.

**Status and support.** Version, stability, supported platforms or accelerators, and whether the project calls itself experimental. A README that says 'research code' is telling you something load-bearing.
**What the README does not cover.** Almost everything: a landing page links outward. Name what it defers to rather than reaching for it -- the links are not yours to follow.
trap_title: The trap: a README is an advertisement
trap: It is written to attract users, so it states intent as achievement and elides what does not work. The feature list is a plan as often as it is a description, and the benchmark in the header was measured on hardware and at a shape the page may not name. Report what it claims as a claim, attach whatever configuration it gives, and where it gives none, say the figure is unattributed rather than passing it on as a property of the project. A repo root is also the *least* specific page in a repository: if `{keyword}` is a particular API or kernel, the honest answer is usually that this page mentions it and does not document it.
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by reading like the project's own marketing: fluent, enthusiastic, and no more informative than the README, with a roadmap item reported as a shipped feature.

lead: This is a research paper. The entry is its **claim, the method behind it, and the configuration its numbers were measured at** -- in that order. A paper is not documentation: nothing in it is a supported interface, and its results describe one setup on one set of hardware at one date. Lead with what the paper argues, not with what the subject is.
extract: **The claim, as the abstract states it.** What the authors say they show, in their terms, including the hedges. 'Up to', 'on our workloads' and 'compared to a baseline of' are the parts a later reader most needs and the first to be dropped.
**The method, at the level that makes the result mean something.** Enough that a reader can tell what was actually done -- not a restatement of the architecture section.

**Every number with the configuration it was measured at.** Hardware, topology, model size, batch, sequence length, precision, and the baseline it is relative to. A speedup without its baseline is not a result; a throughput without its shape is not a number. Where the paper omits one, report the figure as unattributed rather than as a property of the technique.
**Limits the paper states about itself.** Its own future-work and threats-to-validity sections, which say what it does not establish.
**Version and date.** Papers are revised; arXiv v1 and v3 can differ in their numbers. Give what this version says.
trap_title: The trap: a result is not a recommendation
trap: The gap between 'this worked in this experiment' and 'do this' is the whole distance between a paper and a playbook, and an entry that closes it silently is the most damaging thing this index can produce -- it reads like guidance and carries none of the conditions. Do not convert a measured result into advice. Do not generalise from the hardware tested to hardware that was not. Where a technique is a research prototype rather than something shipped, say so: a reader planning against it needs to know whether they can actually use it.
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by turning findings into instructions: the hedges gone, the baseline gone, the topology gone, and a conditional result restated as a rule about TPUs.

lead: This source documents one project across several accelerators, and we run on TPU. Report `{keyword}` as it applies to TPU, and say so where it does not apply at all.
extract: **What the setting is** -- name, type, default, and what reads it, in the source's own words.

**Which platform it is for.** Say it for every item: TPU, or CUDA/ROCm only, or platform-neutral. A reader on TPU acting on a CUDA-only setting changes nothing and concludes the setting does not work.

**How the source says so** -- the guard that proves it, quoted or named: a `current_platform.is_tpu()` branch, a CUDA-only import, a docstring that names the backend, a ROCm-only default. Platform from evidence, never from the name.
Leave out what is plainly for another accelerator unless the question asked for it. A long list of CUDA settings buries the two that matter here.
trap_title: The trap: the name does not say the platform
trap: Most of these names carry no accelerator in them, and the few that do are not the ones that matter -- vllm/envs.py names ROCm 95 times and CUDA 42 against 9 for TPU, while only two variables have TPU in the name. So a setting that looks generic is usually read by one backend, and reporting it unqualified tells a TPU reader to set something nothing on their machine will read. Where the source does not say which platform, write that it does not say. `applies to: not stated` is a useful entry; a platform you inferred from the name is not.
fails_by: This kind of entry fails by being *comprehensive* -- every setting listed, every default right, and most of them belonging to a different accelerator.
